rationale: A wins because it knows where the floorboards are weak and mostly refuses to step through them. Its proof gate, "whether $342K represents savings identified...or savings realized," is exactly the question a finance reporter asks before wasting a Tuesday. B has sharper instincts, but "plans to charge enterprises later" and "They came from cancelling" assert facts the update does not give; that is how a clever angle becomes a correction.
gaps_in_A: "Ramp Turns Its $80 Billion Payments Network Into a Procurement Intelligence Engine" puts strategy varnish on a fact that only says Ramp processes $80B and the agent scans spend; the claimed intelligence advantage needs proof before it becomes a headline.
"the first public signal of Ramp explicitly turning payment data into procurement intelligence" invents both "first" and "explicitly." The update gives a launch, not a public-strategy milestone.
"The Enterprise AI Agent That Insists Humans Stay in the Loop" oversells a simple approval gate with "enterprise" and "insists." The governance idea is good; the headline is dressed for a TED panel.
It buries "the feature is included for existing customers at no extra cost" instead of testing a cleaner platform-bundling angle. That is a real business-model story left half-used.
gaps_in_B: "Ramp gives away software-spend auditing for free, and plans to charge enterprises later" invents the charging claim. The update says an enterprise tier is coming; it does not say paid.

"The AI agent's biggest savings didn't come from negotiating. They came from cancelling." The update says savings came mostly from unused seats and auto-renewals, not that cancellation beat renegotiation.
"software nobody uses" is too cute and too broad. Duplicate seats and auto-renewals are not automatically software nobody uses.
"attacks revenue lines vendors have quietly relied on" assigns vendor dependence and motive without evidence or vendor comment. Plausible is not the same as sourced.
